s75.title: 2910 CAD and Tech Binder Release 2025, post 174

bet.text: Be the well-rounded robot: score every way it can, L1 through L4, and put up as many points as possible in a match.

demand.text: Every level of the reef, then much more L1. After its week five event the team saw that others prioritized L2 to L4 and neglected L1, the level with the fewest points.
The team wanted to excel at a fast hang, six-coral L1 stacks, the lollipop auto and algae in the barge, and assumed it would score only L1 once the algae was gone.

auto.text: At Silicon Valley an analyst described its signature auto, which collects what the analyst calls the pre-loaded items and got all four of its coral.
In the Einstein finals an analyst says 1323 and 2910 chose lollipop autos.
In Einstein finals 2 it alternated L4 and L2 coral: the order suited its slow elevator and left algae in predictable spots.

cycle.text: The ground intake pulls coral in and centers it; a sensor starts the handoff. The end effector scores L2 to L4 from front or back. For L1, both intakes swipe coral onto the reef.
In the Einstein finals an analyst says it scored coral only in L1, leaving the branches to its partners, and picked up algae at times.

endgame.text: Flex wheels pull in the cage's vertical pipe and spring-loaded latches hold it. A proximity sensor starts an automated sequence: the elevator folds, pulling the climber down, and the algae intake latches into the end effector.

fallback.text: The team added a human-loading mode, enough to limp through a match if the ground intake stopped working.

gave_up.text: The robot depended on ground loading, could not pick up coral past 45 degrees, and needed a ton of practice.
The practice robot weighed 130 lb in week 5 of build season.
The 115 lb limit was hard to meet, so the team chose a smaller frame and tested materials to keep structural integrity.

changed.text: The ground intake went through many iterations and was done one or two weeks before the championship; carbon fiber rollers became polycarbonate after breakage.
In Einstein match 11 the algae intake's belt jammed and stopped the coral intake, which shares its motor.
The week three hang winched the algae intake; a 2910-inspired backpack hang replaced it for week five and got faster for the championship.

outcome.text: 53-3-0 in official play; won the Newton division, won the championship; captain of the Newton alliance on Einstein; ranked 3 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 117.93, Newton).

functions.name: Drivetrain
functions.type: swerve with WCP X2i and X2t modules

solves.text: Reduce weight while keeping overall stability

facts.text: Square frame side
Free speed, at 6.48:1
Kraken X60 motors drive and Kraken X44 motors rotate the modules
Spacer blocks lower the drivetrain to about 0.5 in ground clearance
The A-frame base bolts to a nut strip on the top of the swerve plate; the team copied this use of the plate as structure from 4414

solves.text: Support the elevator solidly at full extension and rotate it quickly

facts.text: Turns the elevator from horizontal to vertical in about
A-frame of four 2 x 2 x 1/16 in tubes, mounted directly to the drivetrain
Each gearbox uses one Kraken X44 at 182.25:1, with an encoder geared 1:1 to elevator rotation
The base is a 3/16 in aluminum plate with custom nut plates inside the 2 x 2 in tube, braced by a bent 0.090 in aluminum plate
Two bolts pull a shaft to tension the chain; its 1/2 in hex idler sprocket runs on a needle bearing, which the team says worked well all season
CANcoders set the starting angle, then the motor encoder is used; the code re-seeds the angle if the motor has reset

functions.name: Coral Intake
functions.type: ground roller intake with direct handoff

solves.text: Take coral from most angles on the ground and funnel it to the center

facts.text: Flex wheels on the top roller and grip tape on the bottom roller
Compression on the coral, about
Centers coral passively, then hands off directly into the end effector
Pivot geared to 42.67:1; shares its pivot shaft and roller motor with the algae intake
A diffused proximity sensor detects the coral
After driving at full speed into a wall 20 or more times, the robot could still complete a match with the broken SRPP intake
About 20 in wide between two SRPP plates; 2 in flex wheels on a 1.25 in polycarbonate tube on top, a 1.25 in tube with Cat Tongue below
Centering follows the same principles as 3847's ground intake
Front roller prints and glue failed until the team added aluminum dowels, about 1.5 in of grooved glue area and two plastite screws 1 in from the end
The thin pivot tube (about 0.030 in wall) is bolted to its plug through a much thicker sleeve, so the tube does not rip
The team found SRPP better than polycarbonate, which it has normally had to skin with 0.060 in aluminum to keep from breaking

cost.text: It could not pick up coral past 45 degrees, which took a ton of practice to work around
The effective roller reduction was about 4.6:1; the team would have liked 6:1 to 7:1 but a change also affected the algae intake
Getting the rollers right cost the team many practice days

solves.text: Take algae from the ground over the bumpers and help with L1

facts.text: Custom billet aluminum arms and SRPP plates
2 in polycarbonate roller with grip tape at the center
Pivot geared to 64:1, driven on both sides so both arms move together
Works with the coral intake to score L1
Latches into the end effector to support the drive base when the robot is disabled after climbing
Also winched to hang before the backpack hang; that it could latch the later hang was luck, the team says

solves.text: Start short enough to pivot inside the frame perimeter and still reach L4 and the barge

facts.text: Number of stages
Two internally run 18 mm wide, 5 mm pitch HTD belts
One Kraken X60 through a two-stage gearbox at 6.875:1
Interlocking hard stops on each stage add rigidity at full extension
Height of each stage, about
Lifts about 20 to 30 lb or more, by the team's guess, with no constant force springs on the elevator
Idlers with a 1/2 in hex shaft run on double needle bearings (5/16 x 1/2 in), which the team says helped with friction
The team traced early position drift to belt tension and to wrap on the bottom drive pulley; with a Kevlar belt tensioned enough, it did not skip
A velocity and current check confirms the elevator has reached the bottom

cost.text: It was slower than other teams' and its one motor often stalled; the team would gear it faster with two Kraken X60s if it could
With so many stages they did not slide past each other well; the team lived with it

solves.text: Lower the center of gravity by keeping all motors but one off the end effector

facts.text: Three gearboxes are integrated into the billet plates, to reduce part count
A low-profile belt tensioner for the return belt sits at the bottom; a ratchet plate keeps the belt tension

solves.text: Rotate the end effector with power from gearboxes in the carriage

facts.text: Custom 3D printed bevel gears, each driven by an identical three-stage 61.6:1 gearbox in the carriage
The final reduction is #25H chain
A billet yoke holds two 3.5 in X-contact bearings; hard stops are machined in
Bevel gears are 10 DP with about 0.875 in of tooth face, a guess that did not break
The bevel gears are printed in plain Onyx on the competition robot
CTR differential mode with two CANcoders, one per motor; twist is limited mechanically to 200 degrees
Each encoder must keep 1:1 resolution over the whole motion; the practice robot's did not, and it was painful when zeroed wrong

cost.text: The biggest hurdles were fitting everything in the carriage, belt slip and encoder range; the team would use herringbone bevels next time

solves.text: Take and score coral on every reef level and move algae from the reef to the barge

facts.text: Two independently driven sets of flex wheels move coral horizontally and vertically
Front 3 in flex wheels can pinch algae and are powered through the center of the differential gears
A Kraken X44 drives the vertical rollers at 3:1
A retroreflective sensor on a CANdi detects algae and coral; the team had poor results in the past with sensors wired straight to the roboRIO
The end effector motor on the wrist runs from PWM, for fear of breaking the CAN chain; ID, firmware and current limits are set over CAN first
Front 3 in and rear 2 in wheels differ in durometer: the 3 in wheels spin to open a gap while scoring, and the coral slides out on the 2 in wheels
The 3 in wheels must be stopped while the arm whips the coral around, or the coral flies out
One of the claw motors is a Kraken X60 rather than an X44, because of its stalls and load
The team estimates 20 or more iterations of the claw in the season

cost.text: The hold works until it does not: wheels need replacing at random
Some mechanisms cut through wire shielding quickly; a pneumatic tube over the wires was a mid-season fix

functions.name: Climbing System
functions.type: flex-wheel capture pulled down by the elevator

solves.text: Climb with a combination of elevator, shoulder and algae intake

facts.text: Two 3 in 45A flex wheels, driven by one Kraken X44, bring the cage's vertical pipe into spring-loaded latches
A diffused proximity sensor sees that the cage is latched and starts the automated climb
Slides on linear bushings along 3/4 in tubes, sprung up by a constant force spring and pulled down as the elevator folds
Slides passively so the chain ends up centered over the robot's center of gravity

solves.text: Start the whole handoff from a sensor once the coral is in the intake

facts.text: A Limelight 4 in the A-frame is placed for object tracking, with a shroud against falling coral
Three Limelight 4 cameras: two for AprilTags without the Hailo module, which the team saw perform better, and one with it for object detection
Most of the robot was automatic across its 6 degrees of freedom; the co-driver picks the level and the driver picks the left or right pole of the nearest face
In auto it tracks the algae and its height to confirm the coral is there and generate a new path; a clean grab allowed only about 1 in of error
It aligns to the AprilTag on each reef face, not to the pole
Automatic release was tried, but the team found scoring cleaner with the driver triggering it, because of the robot's quirks
A choreographer compares current and wanted positions, picks the order of moves by simple heuristics and returns a command sequence
The choreographer can slow a mechanism: the elevator pivots at very low acceleration when fully extended, and climb speeds were tuned until it always latched
For the championship it added a Limelight so it could also auto score L1

cost.text: The robot had many tight clearances and spots where it could get stuck, which the team had to automate around

solves.text: Get the robot down to the 115 lb limit

facts.text: Cuts: SRPP plates, more pocketing, plastic or titanium bolts for steel, thinner aluminum, drilled shafts, thinner wire, stub rollers and prints for metal or solid plastic
The faces of drivetrain tubes that point into the robot are pocketed; the outer faces stay whole
1x1, 2x1 and 2x2 tubing has mainly 0.060 in wall, which the team calls the right combination of strength and weight
12 and 14 AWG wire and thin-insulation Alpha wire let the energy chain shrink from 15 x 30 mm to 15 x 15 mm
Spoked instead of pocketed 84T gears save about 0.06 to 0.07 lb each; the team has seen no failures with a sprocket as the final reduction
Parts are pocketed aggressively on the practice robot, then thickened or pocketed more depending on how they hold up

cost.text: Pocketing tubes was a risk taken on gut judgment; the team advises 0.060 and 0.090 in tube, pocketed only as a last resort
In 2026 the team said its thin-insulation Alpha wire costs more and is less flexible than silicone wire

decisions.because: the pivoting elevator had to start short inside the frame perimeter, so stages were added to regain height, and the team wants more than enough reach
decisions.instead_of: fewer stages on a much longer robot

decisions.because: the weight limit was hard to meet
the team judged it very easy to do
decisions.instead_of: the winch climb it used in the past
decisions.cost: about 5 lb, against about 4 lb for the earlier hang

decisions.because: it lowers the center of gravity; one motor sits beyond the carriage
other teams had prioritized L2 to L4 and neglected L1

decisions.choice: No indexer or centering stage behind the ground intake
decisions.because: it was too hard in prototypes and the team worried about robustness
decisions.cost: coral past 45 degrees could not be picked up

decisions.choice: X2i modules on the elevator side and X2t on the intake side
decisions.because: X2i weighs less and X2t leaves more clearance for the intake gearboxes

decisions.choice: Print the practice robot in PETG and the competition robot in Onyx
decisions.because: PETG is affordable, fast and fails earlier, so weak parts show up before an elimination run; the team adds it would probably do for most competition parts
one of its main designers wanted to build it
decisions.instead_of: a robot in the style of 1690 and 2056, already drawn
decisions.cost: the concept was fixed at the end of week 2; the team normally aims for the end of week 1

decisions.because: it could score L1 cleanly or hand off for L2 to L4, and the team expected to score only L1 at the highest level
decisions.instead_of: picking up coral with the end effector

decisions.choice: One motor for the coral and algae intakes
decisions.because: there was no weight left for a motor each
decisions.cost: when the algae intake belt jammed, the coral intake failed too

decisions.choice: Remove the suction mechanism that held algae
decisions.because: it saved 4 lb of the 15 lb the team needed to lose
decisions.cost: the suction had let it carry algae around on the claw

decisions.choice: Chain for rotating joints: 25 for low load, 35 for higher
decisions.because: belts and spur gears on pivots disappointed the team before; chain has been robust and stiff

decisions.choice: Two Kraken X44s on the shoulder
decisions.because: a bit more stall torque and better response
crimped power lug and 24 slots; the same port on its REV board had failed twice and fused power ports four times in two years

decisions.choice: Detailed block CAD as the master model
decisions.because: with pivots, sizes and space fixed, assemblies can be designed and made in parallel, with room to grow or shrink
